item.title: Beyond Fidelity: Evaluating Synthetic Medical Imaging Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.28154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of synthetic medical imaging datasets (SMD) in the development and evaluation of machine learning models has motivated interest in systematic methods to assess dataset quality across different imaging modalities. Common evaluation strategies rely heavily on fidelity-oriented metrics developed for general computer vision and may not capture clinically relevant properties such as anatomical plausibility, dataset coverage, metadata completeness, subgroup consistency, or documentation quality. We present the ScoreCard Toolkit that operationalizes six of the seven dimensions found within the 7Cs approach for SMD evaluation across Congruence, Coverage, Completeness, Consistency, Constraint, and Comprehension. The ScoreCard Toolkit provides a modular pipeline for preprocessing, feature extraction, metric computation, visualization, and structured scorecard generation. This approach complements standard fidelity-based evaluation by exposing quality characteristics not captured by those measures alone, including constraint violations, anatomically implausible shape artifacts, and metadata-related consistency issues. The toolkit supports appearance, texture, and shape features and is designed to accommodate additional feature representations, including radiomic features, deep-learning embeddings, and foundation-model representations. We demonstrate the end-to-end workflow across three imaging modalities: synthetic digital pathology whole-slide image patch data, synthetic digital mammography, and synthetic head CT. Across all three modalities, the resulting scorecards reveal dataset-specific quality characteristics, such as distributional biases and coverage gaps that may impact their effectiveness for model development or testing. ScoreCard provides a practical, extensible, and modality-agnostic approach for evaluating and transparently reporting SMD quality.
item.dc:creator: Seyed Kahaki, Alexander R. Webber, Tahsin Rahman, Elim Thompson, Jana Delfino, Aldo Badano

item.title: Which Vertebral Landmark Errors Change a Cobb Angle? Geometry-Weighted Supervision for Radiographic Landmark Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.28156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A network that localizes vertebral corners can reduce pixel error while rotating the line used to measure spinal curvature. We derive a training loss from the geometry of a three-angle reader. Of the eight corner-displacement degrees of freedom of a vertebral quadrilateral, one local direction rotates its left-to-right chord. The angular sensitivity in this direction is inversely proportional to chord width. An orthonormal Hadamard basis lets us give this residual extra weight during training while retaining supervision on the other seven directions. In five-fold image-level development experiments on 372 anteroposterior radiographs, we compared three objectives across 45 fits of the same landmark network. The three-seed corner ensemble reduced pooled symmetric percentage error from 18.45% with coordinate supervision to 17.20% with geometry weighting. Adding a soft pairwise-angle term yielded 16.89%, a paired difference of $-1.56$ percentage points from coordinate supervision (95% image-bootstrap interval $[-2.51,-0.61]$). The interval for the increment from adding the soft term included zero. In a single-fold comparison, direct unit-chord supervision also reduced error, and its difference from geometry weighting was uncertain. Across single-seed runs, rotational residual error fell by 36.1% while normalized corner error rose from 2.60% to 2.71%. Perturbing one vertebra at a time also showed when a small rotation changes the selected end pair. These results identify a measurable trade-off between landmark fidelity and agreement with a specified geometric reader. The evaluation concerns an internal image-level split and landmark-derived target angles.
item.dc:creator: Zizhao Peng

item.title: Duplicate- and Patient-Overlap Leakage in Brain MRI Tumor Classification: A Multi-Model Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.28161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background. Repeated MRI images and distinct slices from the same patient can both compromise evaluation of brain tumor classifiers. Objective. We audited image duplication and examined how patient overlap relates to discrimination, probability error and model ranking. Methods. The Cheng/Figshare dataset contains 3,064 contrast-enhanced T1 MRI slices, three tumor classes and 233 recorded patient IDs. The dataset author advised treating the IDs as individuals, but original DICOM records were unavailable for verification. Four CNN architectures were trained under image-level and recorded-ID-disjoint protocols with five folds matched on size and class counts (40 original runs). A patient-cluster bootstrap quantified uncertainty. The extension added 60 split-seed runs, 40 training-seed runs and 72 fixed-test sibling-exposure runs with class-matched other-patient controls. Results. We found no exact duplicate images and little evidence of cross-patient near-duplicates among screened pairs. Image-level minus recorded-ID-disjoint balanced accuracy ranged from +0.0318 to +0.0462 across models. Expected calibration error and multiclass Brier scores were lower on the image-level evaluation sample. The balanced-accuracy difference persisted across new seeds for ResNet50 and DenseNet121, but their original ranking reversal did not replicate. Only ResNet50 in fold 2 passed Holm correction in the five-test exposure family. All 16 correlated exploratory subgroup estimates were positive, with no consistent dose-response. Conclusions. Patient overlap was associated with higher apparent performance on this benchmark. Fixed-test comparisons could not isolate patient identity from shared anatomy or acquisition characteristics. No independent external clinical validation was performed.
item.dc:creator: Xin Li, Samson Oluwadare

item.title: The UNIFESP Chest CT Fatty Liver Dataset
item.description: arXiv:2611.28164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hepatic steatosis is common, usually asymptomatic, and frequently visible on CT examinations performed for other reasons, including chest CT, in which the upper abdomen is partly included. We describe the UNIFESP Chest CT Fatty Liver Dataset, a public collection of 285 unenhanced CT studies (344 series, 99,883 images) from 264 patients examined at a single academic center in Brazil: 152 patients with chest CT and 112 patients with abdominal CT. Each patient has a binary label for the presence of hepatic steatosis, assigned by a radiology resident who compared the attenuation of three regions of interest in the liver with one in the spleen. Images are provided in de-identified DICOM format. The dataset was used in the UNIFESP Chest CT Fatty Liver Competition, hosted on Kaggle in 2022, with 226 patients for training and 38 patients with chest CT for testing. In a technical validation, the criterion of liver attenuation lower than spleen attenuation, measured automatically, agreed with the labels in 206 of the 226 training patients (91%). The dataset is available at https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/unifesp-fatty-liver.
item.dc:creator: Augusto Sarquis Serpa, Mariana Ramos Scolari, Eduardo Moreno Judice de Mattos Farina, Eduardo Caminha Nunes, Felipe Matsuoka, Felipe Campos Kitamura, Nitamar Abdala

item.title: Quality-Control Policies Shape Model Behaviour in Computational Pathology
item.description: arXiv:2611.28179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quality-control policies determine which image regions are used by computational pathology models, but their effects are difficult to isolate when quality estimation and input selection are coupled. We make these policies explicit, configurable and testable. We introduce PathQC-3C, comprising 1,661 densely annotated regions from 1,194 haematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images across 32 cancer/tissue categories, and TileNet, a framework that separates dense tissue/background/artefact estimation from task-specific input-selection policies. We evaluated the default predictor across three held-out cohorts and against harmonised quality-control comparators, assessed policy decisions in a blinded single-pathologist audit, and tested alternative policies in three downstream settings. In retrospective CAMELYON16 multiple-instance learning, background-aware selection improved the pooled out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.758 to 0.839 compared with random sampling from the same exhaustive candidate pool under a fixed tile budget. In weak-label lung classification, strict artefact exclusion reduced the pre-matching candidate pool by approximately 43%, with small metric-dependent differences after matching training-set size and patient contribution. PathQCAug, which composites real artefact components during tumour-stroma model adaptation, improved macro Dice on high-artefact tiles under severe held-out composited artefacts across three training seeds and outperformed random-erasing and clean-tissue controls. Separating quality estimation from policy execution provides an auditable way to control which image content enters computational pathology models; the appropriate policy is task specific, and clinical utility remains to be established.
item.dc:creator: Mario Parre\~no Centeno, Yu Guan, Pedro Montero Pav\'on, Sanna Palosaari, Juha V\"ayrynen

item.title: Beyond Outlier Rejection: Transient-Aware Reconstruction of Multi-Stack MRI
item.description: arXiv:2611.28184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical MRI typically acquires the organ of interest as consecutive stacks of 2D slices in different orientations. Reconstruction methods such as SVRTK and NeSVoR fuse them into one volume and down-weight what does not fit, although in living tissue the change during the scan is often the signal itself and can contain clinically relevant physiological information, such as fetal motion and uterine contraction. We propose an analysis-by-synthesis decomposition that explains every acquired voxel through its exact acquisition geometry as a static anatomy shared by all stacks, a rigid and smooth non-rigid motion per stack, and a sparse transient field per stack for changes during one acquisition only. A robust reweighting keeps such changes out of the anatomy. The model is fitted per subject without training data, with one configuration for all datasets. On a digital phantom with known ground truth, static changes are kept entirely in the anatomy, and the transient field of the stack that saw a transient recovers 68% of it at 12mm radius. From identical inputs, the anatomy predicts held-out stacks better than SVRTK and NeSVoR on uterine (NCC 0.897 against 0.874 and 0.863, 123 patients) and on prostate MRI from unseen sites and scanners (0.847 against 0.795 and 0.757, 85 patients), and on fetal brain MRI as well as SVRTK and better than NeSVoR (0.771 against 0.763 and 0.747, 83 fetuses). The transient fields flag corrupted fetal slices with an AUROC of 0.94 against expert raters. As the input of a frozen anomaly detector trained on healthy subjects only, the anatomy localizes radiologist-delineated uterine lesions better than the SVRTK and NeSVoR volumes (AUROC 0.76 against 0.71 and 0.71, 37 patients).
item.dc:creator: Anika Knupfer, Maximilian Lindholz, Maria Camila Bustos-Vivas, Joseph V. Hajnal, Bodo Rosenhahn, Jana Hutter

item.title: EID-Net: Endoscopic Illumination-aware Degradation Correction Network
item.description: arXiv:2611.28198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Endoscopic images captured under complex illumination conditions often suffer from spatially non-uniform exposure degradation, including local under-exposure, over-exposure, and illumination-induced color variation. These degradations are usually entangled with tissue structures, making it challenging for general-purpose low-light enhancement and image restoration methods to improve visibility while preserving local structural and chromatic cues. In this paper, we propose EID-Net, an endoscopic illumination-aware degradation correction network for structure-preserving endoscopic illumination correction. Rather than treating illumination correction as a global intensity adjustment, EID-Net explicitly extracts an endoscopy-oriented degradation prior from the input image to characterize illumination-related variations in a unified representation. This prior is then introduced into the decoder through an illumination-modulated transposed attention mechanism, where it adaptively guides feature aggregation by modulating the key-value feature subspace. Extensive experiments on CEC, Endo4IE, EndoVis17, and EndoVis18 datasets demonstrate that EID-Net performs favorably against recent endoscopic enhancement and general image restoration methods. The code is available at https://github.com/JUNZHIlius/EID-Net.
item.dc:creator: Junzhi Liu, Yinghao Zeng, Yang Liu, Huafeng Li, Xiaosong Li

item.title: US-Seg: One Reference for Universal Ultrasound Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.28740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent ultrasound foundation models have demonstrated strong feature extraction capabilities across organs, tasks, and imaging conditions. However, converting these representations into segmentation still requires finetuning on annotated target data. To reduce reliance on task-specific finetuning, existing universal ultrasound segmentation methods typically adopt prompt-based target specification, mainly through spatial prompts in SAM-style models or task prompts exemplified by MOFO. Yet, directly segmenting targets unseen during training still requires repeated per-image interaction or target-specific adaptation. We propose US-Seg, a universal ultrasound segmentation framework that uses only a single annotated reference to specify the target and directly predicts its mask in query images without finetuning. The fundamental insight of US-Seg is to reformulate segmentation from direct image-to-label mapping for predefined targets into a shared structural recovery process learned from heterogeneous reference-query pairs through masked label reconstruction, thereby making a single reference sufficient for target specification. Boundary-centric label masking emphasizes ambiguous boundaries, encouraging transferable structural cues rather than target-specific appearance patterns. Using these structure-enriched representations, multi-level bidirectional reference-query interaction aligns the reference-defined target with the query. Finally, a prediction-aware iterative decoder uses intermediate predictions to progressively correct residual structural errors under reference guidance. Without repeated interaction or laborious annotation, US-Seg achieves an average Dice of 81.85% across six evaluations covering cross-site and cross-task generalization, outperforming the strongest label-reference method by 24.30%, while also delivering the best in-domain performance.
item.dc:creator: Chen Ma, Yunshu Li, Shuyu Liang, Qin Wang, Junhu Fu, Zeju Li, Yi Guo, Yuanyuan Wang

item.title: Rate-Quality-Energy Convex Hull for High Dynamic Range Adaptive Video Streaming
item.description: arXiv:2611.28817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High Dynamic Range (HDR) video introduces substantially higher decoding complexity and energy consumption than Standard Dynamic Range (SDR), yet most adaptive streaming pipelines still rely on bitrate ladders optimized using SDR-oriented metrics such as VMAF. These ladders fail to capture HDR-specific perceptual behavior and ignore decoder-side energy, resulting in energetically inefficient operating points. This work proposes a rate-quality-energy convex-hull optimization framework that jointly considers bitrate, HDR-aware perceptual quality (HDRVMAF), and client-side processing energy, including decoding and upscaling. Experiments on twelve 4K HDR sequences from the LIVE HDR Video Quality Assessment Database evaluate 72 representations per clip and demonstrate that traditional VMAF-optimized ladders frequently select high-resolution encodes that become dominated once energy is accounted for. Compared to the Default HLS ladder, our HDR-aware method achieves substantial bitrate savings of up to 54.34% at equal HDRVMAF, while yielding relative client-side energy reductions of up to 43.10% under higher energy weighting. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework as a practical foundation for constructing HDR bitrate ladders that explicitly expose and control perceptual quality-energy trade-offs.
item.dc:creator: Amritha Premkumar, Christian Herglotz

item.title: Beyond the section plane: Robust 3D reconstruction of multiplex immunofluorescence exposes limitations of 2D spatial cell statistics
item.description: arXiv:2611.28905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial analysis of the tumour microenvironment with multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) typically relies on single thin tissue sections, which misrepresent the 3D tissue organisation and bias spatial cell statistics in ways that remain largely unquantified. We reconstruct 24 breast and lung tumour tissue microarray cores in 3D, each from 15-20 serial mIF sections, and compare spatial cell statistics in 3D with those from individual sections. Our pipeline combines affine pre-alignment with dense deformable refinement using RoMa v2, achieving a median target registration error of 1.79 $\mu$m, well below nuclear size, which allows nuclei to be linked across sections. While cell-type proportions are preserved in 2D (Pearson corr. $r \geq 0.99$), 3D analysis reveals up to 3.8 times shorter nearest-neighbour distances, 13-19% higher neighbourhood entropy, and 2-4 times more contacts per cell. Tissue composition can thus be reliably estimated from individual sections, whereas cell-cell interactions require volumetric analysis.
item.dc:creator: Junming Ma (Department of Information Technology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden), Olle Edgren Sch\"ullerqvist (Department of Information Technology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden, SciLifeLab, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden), Hui Yu (Department of Immunology, Genetics and Pathology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden), Carina Strell (Department of Immunology, Genetics and Pathology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden), Patrick Micke (Department of Immunology, Genetics and Pathology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden), Joakim Lindblad (Department of Information Technology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden, SciLifeLab, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden), Artur Mezheyeuski (Vall d'Hebron Institute of Research & Institute of Oncology, Barcelona, Spain), Nata\v{s}a Sladoje (Department of Information Technology, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden, SciLifeLab, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden)

item.title: Neural Grey: Practical Vignetting Calibration from Casual Camera Rolls
item.description: arXiv:2611.28934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural Grey estimates a reusable camera-lens shading map from four approximate roll captures of a static, light-colored surface. Rolling the camera moves wall illumination across the sensor while lens shading stays fixed. We fit these two fields jointly, together with small pose and exposure errors, using a physical shading envelope and compact bounded neural residuals. Rotation alone, however, cannot distinguish radial lens attenuation from radial wall illumination. A focal-conditioned radial selector addresses this ambiguity: it uses focal length and sensor size to choose the broad radial profile while retaining the fitted spatial remainder. Component and sensitivity studies separate the roles of the field representation, radial selection, and numerical settings. Neural Grey reaches 25.43 dB on 100 synthetic cases, 24.49 dB on ray-traced lens architectures, and 25.38 dB on 21 real takes from seven optical configurations. On the real benchmark, it exceeds the strongest competing mean by 5.62 dB and wins five of seven configurations.
item.dc:creator: Yueze Wang, Spencer LaVere Smith

item.title: 3D-EMCAD: Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoding for Volumetric Brain Tumor Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encoder-decoder networks are widely used for volumetric brain tumor segmentation, yet recent trends favor high-capacity decoders that incur steep computational costs in 3D at high spatial resolutions. The Efficient Multi-scale Convolutional Attention Decoder (EMCAD) is a lightweight decoder that achieves strong accuracy at very low cost, but it has been validated only in 2D. Here, we extend EMCAD to volumetric segmentation (3D-EMCAD) by converting all operations to 3D and replacing standard normalization layers with group normalization to suit the small batch sizes of volumetric training. To isolate the impact of decoder choice, we evaluate five decoders: the proposed 3D-EMCAD, a vanilla SegResNet decoder, an Attention U-Net decoder, UNet++, and a plain U-Net decoder using an identical 3D SegResNet encoder and training protocol on BraTS 2020 (369 cases, three-fold cross-validation). The five decoders yield statistically indistinguishable performance: their mean Dice scores span only 0.0071, less than the fold-to-fold variation of most models, and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test shows no significant difference between 3D-EMCAD and three of the four baselines. Importantly, 3D-EMCAD achieves this shared accuracy with the fewest decoder parameters (1.15 M) and operations (8.6 G), requiring $7.3\times$ fewer operations than UNet++, which scores no higher. These findings demonstrate that decoder capacity beyond a modest budget offers no measurable benefit for volumetric brain tumor segmentation.
item.dc:creator: Iftakhar Hossain, Israt Jahan Sinthia, Md. Hadiur Rahman Khan

item.title: Where does pancreatic lesion segmentation fail on public CT? An attenuation-stratified analysis of a duct-guided pipeline on PanTS
item.description: arXiv:2611.29861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lesion segmentation is a building block of most CT pipelines for pancreatic cancer detection, yet lesion overlap scores stay low. Instead of proposing a new architecture, we report where an end-to-end pipeline fails on a large public dataset. On PanTS we built a three-stage pipeline: pancreas segmentation, maps of the main pancreatic duct (MPD) and common bile duct (CBD), and a lesion model that receives the CT with or without the predicted duct maps. Both lesion models were trained identically on 4007 scans and evaluated once on 737 held-out test scans (127 with a lesion) under a comparison rule fixed before the test run. Lesion Dice was 0.213 with duct maps and 0.209 with CT only (paired difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.011 to +0.019). The duct maps raised the share of lesions touched by a prediction (+0.079, 95% CI +0.024 to +0.134) but also enlarged predictions in lesion-free scans, and lesion-like regions were predicted in all lesion-free test scans. Out of fold, keeping only the predicted components that touched the lesion raised Dice only from 0.285 to 0.309; the loss came mainly from the extent of correctly located predictions. Clearly hypoattenuating lesions, which intensity alone separates from normal pancreas, had the lowest coverage (median 16.6%). From the predicted maps alone, the MPD diameter separated lesion from lesion-free test scans with AUC 0.794 (95% CI 0.747 to 0.839), while the CBD diameter was weak (AUC 0.603) and added nothing. Code for training, inference and evaluation is publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Kang-Won Byun

item.title: Generalizable Variable-Rate Adaptation for Image Coding for Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.29914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image Coding for Machines (ICM) aims to preserve task-relevant information for machine vision under limited bitrates. However, most ICM models are trained for a fixed operating point, and extending them to variable-rate compression is challenging because their training objectives differ across tasks and model designs. In this paper, we propose a loss-agnostic distillation framework for variable-rate ICM. A pretrained fixed-rate ICM model is used as a frozen teacher, while a student model learns variable-rate behavior through importance-adaptive quantization and distillation-based optimization. This enables continuous bitrate control with a single model while preserving task-relevant latent components, without requiring the original task-specific loss or downstream task labels. Experiments based on existing ICM models demonstrate that the proposed method provides continuous bitrate control and achieves competitive recognition performance compared with the fixed-rate models.
item.dc:creator: Yui Tatsumi, Hiroshi Watanabe

item.title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
item.description: arXiv:2611.30198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.
item.dc:creator: Parastoo Farajpoor, Mohammadreza Narimani

item.title: Demographic Encoding is Not Exposure: Fairness and Privacy in Chest X-ray Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.31014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical foundation models encode patient demographics and can reveal whether a patient was in the training set, and these properties are often treated as one problem. We tested whether they are aligned by measuring demographic encoding, diagnostic fairness gaps and membership-inference vulnerability on the same models. We trained 200 linear or multilayer-perceptron (MLP) heads on frozen BiomedCLIP, DINOv2 and RAD-DINO embeddings, with three seeds, and audited them on CheXpert and NIH ChestX-ray14. Demographic encoding explained almost no variance in patient vulnerability, and all 72 CheXpert associations were statistically equivalent to zero. Erasing linearly decodable demographics left leakage unchanged but reduced age-related underdiagnosis gaps. Leakage depended instead on head capacity and training length. On RAD-DINO, a linear head reached a membership-inference area under the curve (AUC) of 0.694, compared with 0.907 for a 30-epoch MLP, at similar test performance. Fairness and privacy should therefore be audited separately, and linear heads or shorter training reduce leakage with little or no loss of utility. The code is available on GitHub for public use.
item.dc:creator: Sahar Askari, Amin Golnari

item.title: Temporal Persistence for Stylized Rendering: Historical Image Storage and Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.28114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The overlapping silhouettes and gradual fading in The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask (released April 27, 2000) produce a distinctive depiction of motion blur, in which earlier scene states remain visible as part of the current image. Reproducing this appearance in a modern renderer involves decisions about when historical images are sampled, how their contributions are retained, and how the resulting history can be represented within the available memory and processing budget. In this paper, we investigate these decisions through complete image histories, shared image regions, and selectively retained pixel changes, using Godot engine implementations evaluated against independently composited references. For a ten-image history sampled at 20 Hz on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti, half-float storage halves history allocation and reduces median storage-pass duration by factors of 2.40 at 720p and 1.73 at 1080p, preserving the supplied source precision. The adaptive experiments examine how memory savings depend on reconstruction metadata and allocation, including a sparse representation that reduces allocation by 83.81% at low resolution with 445.25 times the GPU duration.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Szelogowski

item.title: Separating Module Gain From Transport Plan Contribution in Audio-Visual Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.28120v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.
item.dc:creator: Vu Nhat Minh Pham, Cong Khanh Nguyen, Minh Tuan Le, Van Thong Huynh

item.title: Simple Baselines for Fetal Brain Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.28505v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) offers a promising approach to fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis, where pathological data are scarce. Existing methods rely mainly on brain age prediction or image reconstruction, but are limited by noisy gestational age (GA) labels, lack of lesion localization, or poor cross-domain generalization. We propose FetalBUAD, a UAD framework based on voxel-level brain age estimation. A joint multi-task network predicts global brain age, voxel-level brain age maps, and brain segmentation to establish an internal biological brain age reference, reducing reliance on clinically recorded GA. Uncertainty-aware voxel-level brain age gap maps are then used for anomaly localization. Experiments on 1,317 internal fetal brain MRI volumes and an external benchmark demonstrate state-of-the-art anomaly detection performance and improved cross-domain generalization. FetalBUAD also generates anatomically interpretable maps that localize diverse fetal brain abnormalities. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/birthlab/FetalBUAD.
item.dc:creator: Hongjia Yang, Mingxuan Liu, Yingqi Hao, Xiaotian Hu, Siyao Li, Xuguang Bai, Fenglin Jia, Yijin Li, Yifei Chen, Zihan Li, Juncheng Zhu, Jing Liu, Yi Liao, Ziyu Li, Haibo Qu, Qiyuan Tian

item.title: SemGuard: Semantics-Decoupled Watermarking for Gaussian Splatting
item.description: arXiv:2611.28636v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gaussian Splatting provides an efficient representation for high-fidelity rendering of static and dynamic 3D scenes, motivating the copyright protection of Gaussian assets. In CLIP-guided Gaussian watermarking, a universal message decoder pretrained on textual watermark representations is subsequently applied to visual features containing both watermark information and scene-dependent semantics. However, text-only pretraining does not explicitly account for the semantic interference encountered during watermark extraction. To address this challenge, we propose SemGuard, a simple yet effective semantics-decoupled watermarking framework that learns to suppress scene-dependent semantic interference during universal message decoder pretraining. Specifically, SemGuard combines message-related CLIP text features with message-independent visual features extracted from unwatermarked scene images, constructing training representations with controllable semantic interference relevant to the target Gaussian assets. A progressive semantic interference curriculum gradually increases the contribution of visual features, allowing the decoder to first learn reliable message representations and then adapt to increasingly strong scene-dependent semantic interference. After pretraining for a given message length and semantic image pool, the decoder is frozen and reused across multiple Gaussian assets whose visual semantics are covered by the pretraining data. Experiments on static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting assets demonstrate improved rendering fidelity alongside reliable watermark extraction, while evaluations on static assets further show enhanced robustness against image-space distortions.
item.dc:creator: Yingying Shi, Zhong Zhou, Bin Zhou

item.title: A Camera-Based Single-Volume, Monolithic Compton Camera
item.description: arXiv:2611.29116v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A Compton camera measures two events in a detector from individual gamma-rays to reconstruct the radiation source. Conventional scintillator-based Compton cameras consist of two separate scintillator volumes or a single segmented scintillator, resulting in drawbacks regarding detector bulkiness and efficiency. Their scintillator readout techniques struggle to resolve two nearby events in one monolithic scintillator. Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras have recently been proposed for measuring scintillation events in various configurations. SPAD array sensors enable high-resolution photon-counting acquisition at high rates that is easily scalable to millions of pixels. Prior work has explored different optics and measurement arrangements as well as demonstrated measurement of single interaction locations. In this work, we extend these capabilities to demonstrate a practical radiation imaging device in the form of a Compton camera consisting of a SPAD camera and one compact, monolithic scintillator. Our Compton camera prototype successfully reconstructs a gamma-ray source over multiple locations that span a 4$\pi$ steradian field of view. Our approach is able to resolve two simultaneous events in one monolithic scintillator and enables Compton camera devices with compact, monolithic scintillator volumes for enhanced portability.
item.dc:creator: Alex Bocchieri, Devanshi Jain, Andreas Velten

item.title: Rateless Lattice Codes over Fading Wiretap Channels: Finite-Length Secrecy and the Secret-Key Capacity of Degraded Sessions
item.description: arXiv:2611.29177v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In rateless transmission the transmitter keeps sending until the legitimate receiver (Bob) can decode. Over a wiretap channel this has a useful side effect: the eavesdropper (Eve) sees only as many symbols as Bob needs, although the transmitter knows neither channel. We study the secrecy of rateless lattice codes in this setting. First, using a public dither and privacy amplification, we prove a finite-length secrecy bound, in total variation distance, for every channel realization, even if Eve knows all codes and seeds and combines all packets. Second, stopping when Bob acknowledges successful decoding, as in hybrid ARQ, costs at most the logarithm of the number of possible feedback outcomes in secret bits. Third, for degraded sessions with state-based stopping and without a pre-shared key or other public discussion, the secret-key rate of a session cannot exceed its accumulated Gaussian secrecy capacity, and adaptive key generation with shaped rateless lattice codes comes within any $\epsilon>0$ of this limit when Eve's channel states are revealed after the session. If only their statistics are known, choosing the key length after the session guarantees a prescribed secrecy-outage probability. Finally, over block Rayleigh fading with a CRC-based acknowledgement and joint belief-propagation decoding, and with Eve $20$~dB weaker on average, the scheme reaches $59$--$69\%$ of the outage-weighted throughput of an ideal infinite-length secure hybrid-ARQ benchmark for Bob SNRs of $8$--$20$~dB.
item.dc:creator: Hassan Khodaiemehr, Khadijeh Bagheri, Chen Feng

item.title: Model-Assisted Probability of Detection Studies for Image-Based Human Inspection
item.description: arXiv:2611.30032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Establishing a probability of detection (POD) curve is important for assessing the reliability of components in aging systems. Traditional POD studies rely on physical specimens containing representative flaws and human inspectors who record detection results, making such studies costly. This paper demonstrates how appropriately validated physics-based simulation can substantially reduce, and in suitable applications potentially replace, physical POD experiments. We use XRSIM, an X-ray radiographic simulator, to generate weld images containing cracks of varying size, morphology, and location. Flaw characteristics, locations, and the number of flaws per image were randomized, with images containing zero to three flaws. Each simulated flaw is treated as an observational unit contributing flaw-level hit-miss responses. To capture human inspection variability, the images were presented in random order to five inspectors, each of whom inspected the images twice. The resulting data were analyzed using a repeated-measures binary-regression model accounting for flaw-to-flaw, inspector-to-inspector, flaw/inspector-combination, and inspection-to-inspection variability. Bayesian inference was used to estimate the population-mean POD curve, inspector-specific POD curves, and associated statistical uncertainty. Results show that flaw-to-flaw variability dominates, with appreciable differences among inspectors. The study provides a framework for combining physics-based image simulation with controlled human inspection to estimate POD while reducing the experimental burden of physical specimen fabrication.
item.dc:creator: Qizheng Xia, William Q. Meeker, Joseph N. Gray, Qing Li

item.title: Enhancing Diabetic Retinopathy Detection with CNN-Based Models: A Comparative Study of UNET and Stacked UNET Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2411.01251v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diabetic Retinopathy DR is a severe complication of diabetes. Damaged or abnormal blood vessels can cause loss of vision. The need for massive screening of a large population of diabetic patients has generated an interest in a computer-aided fully automatic diagnosis of DR. In the realm of Deep learning frameworks, particularly convolutional neural networks CNNs, have shown great interest and promise in detecting DR by analyzing retinal images. However, several challenges have been faced in the application of deep learning in this domain. High-quality, annotated datasets are scarce, and the variations in image quality and class imbalances pose significant hurdles in developing a dependable model. In this paper, we demonstrate the proficiency of two Convolutional Neural Networks CNNs based models, UNET and Stacked UNET utilizing the APTOS Asia Pacific Tele-Ophthalmology Society Dataset. This system achieves an accuracy of 92.81% for the UNET and 93.32% for the stacked UNET architecture. The architecture classifies the images into five categories ranging from 0 to 4, where 0 is no DR and 4 is proliferative DR.
item.dc:creator: Ameya Uppina, S Navaneetha Krishnan, Talluri Krishna Sai Teja, Nikhil N Iyer, Joe Dhanith P R

item.title: orGAN: A Synthetic Data Augmentation Pipeline for Simultaneous Generation of Surgical Images and Ground Truth Labels
item.description: arXiv:2506.14303v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep learning for surgical image analysis is constrained by limited data diversity, ethical restrictions, high acquisition costs, and the scarcity of accurately annotated bleeding datasets, making reliable bleeding localization particularly challenging. To address these limitations, we propose orGAN, a modular framework that generates realistic, fully annotated synthetic surgical bleeding images together with recoverable point-level supervision. To overcome the ethical and cost barriers of real surgical data, the pipeline is trained on silicone-based mimicking organs that reproduce tissue properties, using an enhanced StyleGAN3 generator coupled with Relational Positional Learning to embed bleeding coordinates, a Surgical Label Detection Algorithm to recover coordinate and mask labels, and a fine-tuned LaMa inpainting network to restore clean image-label pairs. To compensate for scarce annotations, Bleeding Alert Map (BAM) localization models are trained on a blend of synthetic and mimicking-organ images. The enhanced StyleGAN3 attains an Inception Score of 2.24, and the inpainting network preserves realism at a mean SSIM of 0.98. The blended model outperforms both single-source baselines, reaching a Dice coefficient of 0.635 on paired bleeding frames. With a stronger Pix2PixHD backbone, Dice rises to 0.893 with a centroid error of 6.3 pixels. On real Hamlyn surgical video, the blended model achieves a frame-level accuracy of 0.858 and a bleeding-frame detection rate of 0.998 on Hamlyn 2, where all 500 frames were annotated as bleeding-positive. These results show that combining realistic synthetic images with mimicking-organ data is an effective, ethical, and economical strategy for developing surgical AI under limited annotated data.
item.dc:creator: Niran Nataraj, Maina Sogabe, Kenji Kawashima

item.title: Training-Free Continuous Bitrate Control for Scalable Image Coding for Humans and Machines
item.description: arXiv:2606.00158v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous variable-rate compression is highly demanded in real-world applications, but remains underexplored in scalable image coding for humans and machines. In this paper, we propose a training-free variable-rate scalable image coding framework. By adaptively adjusting quantization step sizes based on predicted scale values, the proposed method enables independent and continuous bitrate control for the machine and enhancement layers while preserving important latent information in each layer. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and highlight the importance of bitrate allocation between the two layers.
item.dc:creator: Yui Tatsumi, Hiroshi Watanabe

item.title: Complete virtual unwrapping and reading of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus
item.description: arXiv:2606.29085v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The carbonized papyrus scrolls from Herculaneum preserve the only large-scale library to survive from classical antiquity. Many scrolls have remained unread because physical unrolling risks irreversible damage. Non-invasive imaging offers a route to their texts, yet previous work on sealed Herculaneum scrolls has recovered only localized readings. Here, by combining high-resolution X-ray computed microtomography ($\mu$CT) data acquired on the BM18 beamline at the ESRF with machine-learning-assisted virtual unwrapping, we study three still-closed scrolls. For PHerc. 1667, a remnant of earlier attempts at physical unrolling, we achieve the complete unwrapping and reading of the preserved writing surface, making it the first Herculaneum papyrus read completely by virtual unwrapping. The text was transcribed and cross-verified by nine papyrologists. In PHerc. Paris. 4, the source of the Vesuvius Challenge 2023 Grand Prize text, the high-resolution scan makes ink directly visible in the tomographic volume, allowing 3D ink segmentation and comparison of recovered text with visible deposits. In PHerc. 139, we recover title and author-attribution evidence identifying the scroll as Philodemus, On Gods, Book 8. These results establish a basis for the ongoing, systematic recovery and scholarly study of texts preserved within the still-closed Herculaneum library.

item.title: Analyzing Image Encoder Choices and Graph Homophily in GCN Frameworks for Breast Ultrasound Classification
item.description: arXiv:2607.12054v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Breast ultrasound is widely used for screening, yet automated analysis remains challenging due to speckle noise, acquisition variability, and weak separation of benign and malignant cases in standard ultrasound imaging. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have recently emerged as a promising approach by leveraging relationships among similar patient samples. However, it remains unclear how the choice of image encoder influences graph construction and downstream classification performance. In this work, we systematically evaluate five image encoders spanning convolutional and transformer-based architectures for GCN-based breast ultrasound classification. Image embeddings are used to construct cosine similarity k-nearest-neighbor graphs, which are classified using a single-layer GCN with a linear classification head. Across three patient-wise cross-validation folds, higher-capacity encoders consistently improve graph homophily and downstream classification performance, yielding gains in accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score. Moreover, test-set graph homophily exhibits a strong linear correlation with classification accuracy (R-squared = 0.875), with higher-capacity encoders consistently occupying the high-homophily, high-accuracy region, suggesting that encoder-driven improvements in graph structure are a key mechanism underlying the observed performance gains. On 798 images from two external sources, the encoder ordering was preserved, but accuracy was 0.13-0.21 lower than in cross-validation and the homophily-accuracy association was weaker (R-squared = 0.759). These findings establish encoder selection as a critical factor in graph-based breast ultrasound classification and identify graph homophily as a key indicator linking representation quality to downstream classification performance.
item.dc:creator: Sabahattin Mert Daloglu, Ceren Coskun, Harvey Castro, Soner Hacihaliloglu, Ilker Hacihaliloglu

item.title: Native-Space 3D CarveMix for Multi-Site T1w Stroke Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2608.23882v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Segmenting ischemic stroke lesions on T1-weighted (T1w) MRI acquired across different scanners and protocols without intensity standardization is difficult because lesions are subtle and share intensity characteristics with cerebrospinal fluid. Standard deep learning architectures trained across multiple centers plateau around Dice 0.66, with acute lesions ($\le 7$ days post-stroke) performing substantially worse due to severe sample scarcity. We combine a MedNeXt-L ($k=5$) backbone with on-the-fly 3D CarveMix augmentation that pastes real lesion patches into recipient training patches. By generating synthetic lesion placements dynamically within each fold with subject-level split isolation, the model sees more diverse lesion patterns without requiring pre-generated copies on disk. We evaluate on 1,453 native T1w scans from 55 clinical centers in the ISLES 2026 challenge. MedNeXt-L with CarveMix achieved a mean five-fold cross-validation Dice of 0.648 after 500 epochs. For comparison, the estimated Dice for plain MedNeXt-L at epoch 500 was 0.630, obtained by interpolation from its 1,000-epoch training trajectory.
item.dc:creator: Dexter Wen Jie Teo, Kumaradevan Punithakumar

item.title: Flux Compensation as a Prerequisite for Temporal CT: Per-Bundle Cram\'er-Rao Floors and Estimators That Reach Them
item.description: arXiv:2610.19229v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In Temporal CT (TCT) each detector reading sums the photons of up to three rays. Earlier work measured the resulting per-bundle cost as a Dose Inflation Factor (DIF), using one incident count $N_0$ for all rays and a learned prior trained on one patient; this paper removes both restrictions. N$_0$FC ($N_0$ flux compensation), a bow-tie and tube-current-modulation co-design, approximately equalizes each bundle's detected flux. SNN2 is a bias-corrected, box-projected Gauss-Newton Poisson likelihood iteration. V8c, a neural network trained on 19 patients, corrects SNN2. T2bp, an empirical-Bayes post-processor without trained weights, combines per-bundle Poisson likelihoods with a prior from the patient's own bundles. On 23 non-test volumes, N$_0$FC lowers the per-volume median middle-path Cram\'er-Rao floor, as a DIF, from 23-48 under a flat-fluence baseline to 3.3-6.3 at 35-62% of the baseline's incident photons, near the equal-attenuation 13/3 and 1.4-1.7 times below GE-type bow-ties. For bundles with $X_2<6$ (83%), SNN2 attains this floor (median MSE ratio 1.02); holding air paths at zero, a box-constrained maximum likelihood estimate lowers the ratio to 0.88, and T2bp$\circ$SNN2 to 0.89 (0.74-1.26); T2bp's per-patient prior adds measurably only in the deeper bins (a median 12-29% over all bins). T2bp$\circ$SNN2 beats T2bp$\circ$V8c on three of four N$_0$FC test cells, but trails or ties it on the four N$_0$FC validation volumes. V8c beats SNN2 in distribution under baseline acquisition, gains at most 9% under N$_0$FC (losing 14% on the largest in-distribution test patient), and fails on a patient acquired outside its corpus's exposure rule. Flux compensation, chiefly the bow-tie, is a prerequisite; classical estimation attains the resulting limit. The remaining 3- to 6-fold gap to single-source CT at equal fluence, and the high-attenuation tail, are targets for inter-bundle priors.
item.dc:creator: Guy M Besson

item.title: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level
item.description: arXiv:2611.09854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission measures three-dimensional forest structure with a LiDAR instrument aboard the International Space Station. GEDI observations have geolocation errors of about 10 m, which cause misalignment with other remote sensing data and reduce the accuracy of downstream tasks. Matching GEDI ground elevations against high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) from airborne LiDAR is one way to correct these errors, but such DTMs exist in few regions. To widen this method's applicability, we super-resolved a more widely available low-resolution DTM for elevation matching. We ask whether a super-resolved DTM yields the same correction as a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR DTM and, if not, why. In steep forests of western Japan, we super-resolved an existing 10 m-resolution DTM to 1 m. Additionally fusing a global 30 m-resolution DTM from a different source substantially improved the accuracy. Using the resulting DTM, we corrected GEDI observation positions first by a single offset per ground track, then point by point. For most tracks, the per-track corrections nearly agreed with those from the airborne LiDAR DTM. Point-by-point corrections, however, did not agree. This was because the error of the generated DTM was close to the elevation differences that point-by-point correction must resolve, and most of this error lay at scales that even a 10 m-resolution DTM can represent. Under similar conditions, a super-resolved DTM may be usable in place of a 1 m-resolution DTM for per-track correction, but improving the accuracy, or using it for point-by-point correction as well, requires reducing the error at these scales rather than reproducing fine relief.
item.dc:creator: Natsuki Yuda, Shinichiro Shirota

item.title: Physics-Based Learning of the Wave Speed Landscape in Complex Media
item.description: arXiv:2602.03281v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The propagation of waves through complex, inhomogeneous media is a fundamental challenge across scales, from optics to geophysics. In such environments, the waves reflected by the medium are typically dominated by a random speckle pattern, a complex interference resulting from multiple scattering by fine-scale heterogeneities. While this speckle is traditionally viewed as a source of noise that blurs the medium's structure, it contains rich information about the underlying wave speed landscape. Here, we introduce a physics-based learning framework that reconstructs the velocity distribution from the reflection matrix of the medium. We show how the speckle wave-field can be exploited to probe the focusing quality, serving as an intrinsic guide star to evaluate the local consistency of the velocity model. By representing wave propagation as a differentiable multi-layer network, we leverage optimization tools to solve the inverse problem and infer the wave speed map. We validate this approach through ultrasound experiments in highly scattering tissue-mimicking phantoms and human breast tissues, demonstrating its potential for tumor detection and characterization where standard methods fail. This synergy between wave physics and gradient-based optimization provides a general paradigm for non-invasive tomography in any complex environment where reflection data is available.
item.dc:creator: Baptiste H\'eriard-Dubreuil, Emma Brenner, Benjamin Rio, William Lambert, Foucauld Chamming's, Mathias Fink, Alexandre Aubry

item.title: PoRef-MIL: Plug-and-Play Posterior Refinement for Multiple Instance Learning in QSM-Based Brain Disease Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.19193v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) is a novel quantitative MRI contrast for studying tissue susceptibility changes in brain disorders, including Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple sclerosis (MS). However, small cohorts and the lack of local annotations make developing deep learning models for QSM-based diagnosis challenging. In this work, we propose PoRef-MIL, a weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) framework combining iterative slice relabeling and network retraining with a plug-and-play posterior refinement module (PRM). During training, a 2D dual-branch diagnosis network and a subject-level classifier were alternately trained for five rounds. The classifier was used to update slice pseudo-labels for retraining the diagnosis network. The PRM was applied during inference to refine slice probabilities through bidirectional posterior inference and calculate entropy-derived confidence from the refined probabilities, which was then used in sliding-window scoring to obtain subject-level predictions. PoRef-MIL was evaluated on an in-house PD cohort of 287 participants and a public MS cohort of 150 participants. Compared with eight classification methods, PoRef-MIL achieved the highest mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.942 and 0.872, and accuracies of 0.926 and 0.833, for PD and MS classification, respectively. Ablation experiments were conducted to validate the effectiveness of iterative relabeling and PRM, and the plug-and-play feature of the proposed PRM was also evaluated using four state-of-the-art MIL models. Overall, PoRef-MIL offers a promising approach to QSM-based disease classification in small cohorts without manual slice annotations.
item.dc:creator: Ang Gao, Rui Jin, Yin Liu, Pengfei Rong, Feng Liu, G. Bruce Pike, Hongfu Sun, Yang Gao
